questions.question: Which statement best characterizes the relationship between real skew-symmetric matrices and orthogonal matrices in the context of the Cayley transform?
questions.choice_A: The Cayley transform maps any real skew-symmetric matrix to an orthogonal matrix with determinant +1, provided the transform is defined.
questions.choice_B: Any real skew-symmetric matrix exponentiates to an orthogonal matrix with determinant -1 via the Cayley transform.
questions.choice_C: The Cayley transform maps skew-symmetric matrices to a strict subset of symmetric matrices.
questions.choice_D: Skew-symmetric matrices are themselves orthogonal if and only if their eigenvalues are all imaginary.

questions.question: Let Q be a real skew-symmetric matrix (Q = -Q^T). What is the dimension (number of free parameters) of the space of such Q in n dimensions?
questions.choice_D: n

questions.question: For the Cayley parameterization R = (I + Q)(I - Q)^{-1} with Q = -Q^T, what condition ensures that the mapping is well-defined?
questions.choice_A: Q must be full rank.
questions.choice_B: Q must have spectral radius greater than 1.
questions.choice_C: I - Q must be invertible (no eigenvalue of Q equal to 1).
questions.choice_D: Q must be nilpotent.

questions.question: Why can the Cayley transform not represent reflections in O(n)?
questions.choice_A: Because (I + Q) is always singular when det(R) = -1.
questions.choice_B: Because skew-symmetric matrices cannot parameterize any orthogonal matrices.
questions.choice_C: Because the transform only yields matrices with an eigenvalue of -1, which reflections lack.
questions.choice_D: Because the image of the Cayley transform has determinant +1 and excludes matrices with eigenvalue -1.

questions.question: Which property of skew-symmetric matrices over the reals is always true?
questions.choice_A: They have zero diagonal entries.
questions.choice_B: They are diagonalizable over the reals.
questions.choice_C: Their determinant is always 1.
questions.choice_D: They commute with every orthogonal matrix.

questions.question: When using the Neumann series to approximate (I - Q)^{-1} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} Q^k, what is a sufficient condition for convergence?
questions.choice_A: Q is positive semi-definite.
questions.choice_B: The spectral radius of Q is strictly less than 1.
questions.choice_C: Q is idempotent (Q^2 = Q).
questions.choice_D: Q is orthogonal.

questions.question: For small \|Q\|, which first-order approximation to the Cayley transform R = (I + Q)(I - Q)^{-1} is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: R \approx I + Q
questions.choice_B: R \approx I - Q
questions.choice_C: R \approx I + 2Q
questions.choice_D: R \approx I - 2Q

questions.question: What is a primary numerical concern when computing R = (I + Q)(I - Q)^{-1} directly by forming (I - Q)^{-1} explicitly?
questions.choice_A: Underflow due to the orthogonality of R.
questions.choice_B: Loss of skew-symmetry in Q.
questions.choice_C: Inability to compute gradients through matrix operations.
questions.choice_D: Potential amplification of rounding errors and poor conditioning when inverting (I - Q).

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a limitation of the Cayley parameterization in terms of coverage of O(n)?
questions.choice_A: It covers exactly SO(n) except matrices with eigenvalue -1.
questions.choice_B: It covers O(n) completely.
questions.choice_C: It covers only diagonal orthogonal matrices.
questions.choice_D: It covers only 2D rotations in block-diagonal form.

questions.question: In practice, why is it recommended to compute (I - Q)^{-1} via a linear solve rather than forming the inverse explicitly?
questions.choice_A: Linear solves eliminate the need to store Q.
questions.choice_B: Linear solves are typically more numerically stable and avoid unnecessary floating-point error amplification.
questions.choice_C: Forming the inverse is faster but less accurate, so the trade-off is not favorable.
questions.choice_D: It ensures that det(R) remains exactly +1 in finite precision.

questions.question: Suppose we adopt a block-diagonal parameterization of an orthogonal matrix using k blocks of size b \times b (with kb = n). What is the primary benefit of this approach?
questions.choice_A: It guarantees full expressivity equal to arbitrary n \times n orthogonals.
questions.choice_B: It reduces the need for backpropagation through matrix operations.
questions.choice_C: It reduces parameter count and computational cost from O(n^3) to a sum over smaller O(b^3) block operations.
questions.choice_D: It allows representing reflections within each block.

questions.question: Consider truncating the Neumann series for (I - Q)^{-1} after K terms. For small \|Q\|, what is the typical behavior of the approximation error?
questions.choice_A: It grows linearly with K.
questions.choice_B: It remains constant regardless of K.
questions.choice_C: It decreases super-exponentially with K.
questions.choice_D: It decreases roughly on the order of \|Q\|^{K+1}.

questions.question: Which initialization strategy is most appropriate to start training with an orthogonal layer parameterized by the Cayley transform?
questions.choice_A: Initialize Q = 0 so that R = I.
questions.choice_B: Initialize Q with large random entries to improve exploration.
questions.choice_C: Initialize Q to be symmetric to stabilize training.
questions.choice_D: Initialize R directly and then solve for Q.

questions.question: What is a typical method to enforce skew-symmetry of Q during training despite floating-point drift?
questions.choice_A: Apply QR decomposition to Q after each update.
questions.choice_B: Project Q onto the skew-symmetric subspace by Q \leftarrow (Q - Q^T)/2.
questions.choice_C: Normalize Q to have unit Frobenius norm.
questions.choice_D: Clip the eigenvalues of Q to the unit circle.

questions.question: How does the Cayley transform relate to the matrix exponential \(\exp(\cdot)\) for skew-symmetric matrices?
questions.choice_A: Cayley and the exponential map are identical for all skew-symmetric matrices.
questions.choice_B: The Cayley transform is a first-order Taylor approximation to the exponential map.
questions.choice_C: The Cayley transform is a rational approximation that agrees with the exponential map up to first order around Q = 0.
questions.choice_D: The exponential map cannot produce orthogonal matrices from skew-symmetric inputs.

questions.question: Which statement about block-sharing parameterizations is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: Sharing parameters across blocks increases expressivity while keeping parameter count fixed.
questions.choice_B: Block-sharing reduces parameter count but imposes structural constraints that may limit expressivity.
questions.choice_C: Block-sharing guarantees convergence of the Neumann series for any Q.
questions.choice_D: Block-sharing is necessary to ensure det(R) = -1.

questions.question: Which scenario can make the Cayley transform numerically ill-conditioned in practice?
questions.choice_A: When Q is exactly zero.
questions.choice_B: When Q has small norm and is strictly skew-symmetric.
questions.choice_C: When Q has eigenvalues with real parts close to -1.
questions.choice_D: When (I - Q) becomes nearly singular because Q has eigenvalues close to 1 on the real line.

questions.question: Which statement about determinants in the Cayley parameterization is correct?
questions.choice_A: The Cayley transform yields orthogonal matrices with determinant +1 whenever it is defined.
questions.choice_B: The Cayley transform can produce both determinant +1 and -1, depending on Q.
questions.choice_C: Determinant is not defined for Cayley-transformed matrices.
questions.choice_D: The Cayley transform necessarily yields determinant -1 for odd-dimensional matrices.

questions.question: When approximating (I - Q)^{-1} using a truncated Neumann series in the Cayley transform, which practical trade-off is most relevant?
questions.choice_A: Higher truncation order always reduces runtime without affecting accuracy.
questions.choice_B: Lower truncation order reduces compute but may introduce orthogonality drift in R if Q is not very small.
questions.choice_C: Any truncation preserves exact orthogonality of R.
questions.choice_D: Truncation is unnecessary if Q is skew-symmetric.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about coverage limitations of the Cayley transform is true?
questions.choice_A: It cannot represent any rotation matrices in even dimensions.
questions.choice_B: It cannot represent orthogonal matrices that have an eigenvalue equal to -1, including certain 180-degree rotations.
questions.choice_C: It cannot represent any matrices in SO(n).
questions.choice_D: It can represent reflections but not rotations.

questions.question: In implementing block-diagonal orthogonal layers, which practice improves stability and efficiency?
questions.choice_A: Using very large blocks so that the block-diagonal matrix is close to dense.
questions.choice_B: Reusing parameters across blocks to reduce memory, while monitoring potential expressivity loss.
questions.choice_C: Randomly breaking skew-symmetry to avoid singular (I - Q) solves.
questions.choice_D: Avoiding linear solves in favor of explicit inverses for each block.
